text:
[CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2010.14395v2) combines next-item supervision on original histories with contrastive learning between two augmented views through a shared encoder. Cropping selects a random contiguous subsequence, rather than necessarily retaining the recent suffix. Crucially, its ablation already tests augmentation-only supervised training, SASRec_aug: crop raises HR@20 from 0.0541 to 0.0546 on Sports and 0.0529 to 0.0576 on Yelp; adding contrastive loss reaches 0.0596 and 0.0598. Thus supervised cropping has direct precedent, although an explicitly weighted, same-target suffix auxiliary loss differs from CL4SRec’s main contrastive objective.

[NextItNet](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf) uses causal dilated residual convolutions and jointly predicts next items across sequence positions. Its sub-session ablation concerns additional training examples for GRURec/Caser, rather than suffix augmentation of NextItNet itself. At session length 100, sub-sessions improve MRR@5 from 0.0746 to 0.2086 for GRURec and 0.0084 to 0.2080 for Caser; NextItNet without explicit sub-sessions achieves 0.2583. This establishes strong precedent for subsequence supervision, but does not demonstrate gains from adding a recent-suffix branch to a convolutional encoder.

A particularly close recent precedent is [Pay Attention to Sequence Split (SIGIR 2026), official implementation](https://github.com/KingGugu/SSS4SR), which explicitly supports supervised prefix, suffix, and sliding-window training samples. My assessment: recent-suffix supervision is best positioned as a targeted training regularizer, with limited originality in cropping or shared encoding alone. Its specific contribution would require controlled comparisons of full-history loss, suffix-only training, full-plus-suffix supervision, random contiguous crops, and contrastive augmentation, using matched compute and full-history inference. Existing reported metrics do not establish improvements under the supplied RecHarness protocol.
